title: Distance vs. displacement: path length and straight arrow
summary: Distance counts every meter you walk; displacement only points straight from start to finish. Learn when they match, when they cancel, and how to combine perpendicular legs.

leg_e.label: $d_1$
leg_e.body: The opening segment along the east–west axis. Moving east gives a positive change in $x$.
leg_e.example: Walking $90\text{ m}$ east moves you from $x = 0$ to $x = +90\text{ m}$.

leg_n.label: $d_2$
leg_n.body: A turn at a right angle ($90^\circ$) onto the north–south axis, independent of east–west motion.
leg_n.example: Walking $80\text{ m}$ north sets $\Delta y = +80\text{ m}$.

leg_w.label: $d_3$
leg_w.body: Backtracking along the east–west axis: it **adds** to total [dist:distance], but **subtracts** from eastward [dx:net east–west change].
leg_w.example: Turning $30\text{ m}$ west pulls $x$ back from $+90\text{ m}$ to $+60\text{ m}$.

dx.label: $\Delta x$
dx.meaning: net change in east–west position: +60 m
dx.body: Add signed legs along the $x$-axis using {vectors|vector components}: $+90 - 30 = +60\text{ m}$ east.
dx.example: Two opposite segments along the same line partially cancel.

dy.label: $\Delta y$
dy.meaning: net change in north–south position: +80 m
dy.body: Only the northward leg acts along the $y$-axis, so $\Delta y = +80\text{ m}$ north.

dist.label: $d$
dist.meaning: total path length traveled (scalar), in meters
dist.body: Defined in {dist_disp|distance and displacement}: add the positive length of every leg, regardless of direction.
dist.analogy: The odometer in a car or a step counter on your phone—it never runs backward.

disp.label: $\Delta\vec{x}$
disp.meaning: straight-line vector from start to finish, in meters with direction
disp.body: Defined in {dist_disp|distance and displacement}: depends only on start and finish. Its magnitude always satisfies $|\Delta\vec{x}| \le d$.
disp.analogy: A single straight arrow drawn on a map from your starting pin to your ending pin.

pythagoras_disp.title: Combining perpendicular displacements
pythagoras_disp.body: When net horizontal change [dx:$\Delta x$] and net vertical change [dy:$\Delta y$] are perpendicular, they form the legs of a right triangle: $|\Delta\vec{x}| = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = \dfrac{|\Delta y|}{|\Delta x|}$.
pythagoras_disp.example: $\Delta x = 60\text{ m}$ and $\Delta y = 80\text{ m}$ give $\sqrt{60^2 + 80^2} = \sqrt{10000} = 100\text{ m}$ at $\theta \approx 53^\circ$.
pythagoras_disp.useWhen: motion has both east–west and north–south segments.

round_trip.title: Why a round trip has zero displacement
round_trip.body: If you finish at the exact point where you started ($\vec{x}_f = \vec{x}_i$), the arrow from start to finish has length **zero**, so $\Delta\vec{x} = \vec{0}$ even though [dist:distance] $d > 0$.
round_trip.example: One full lap on a $400\text{ m}$ running track gives $d = 400\text{ m}$ and $|\Delta\vec{x}| = 0\text{ m}$.
round_trip.useWhen: an object returns to its starting position.

sections.title: Two ways to answer 'how far?'
sections.body: If you walk around a school building and end up back at the gate, your legs feel every meter—yet you are zero meters from where you began. Physics separates these two questions into {dist_disp|distance and displacement}. [dist:Distance] is a **scalar** (magnitude only) that adds every step; [disp:displacement] is a {vectors|vector} pointing straight from start to finish, and it later drives {speed_vel|velocity} while distance drives {avg_speed|average speed}.

sections.title: Distance and displacement side by side
sections.note: spot the difference before solving any motion problem

head: Property
[dist:Distance] ($d$)
[disp:Displacement] ($\Delta\vec{x}$)
rows: Yes (sign shows direction along an axis)
No, only start and finish matter

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
Starting from the school gate, a student walks [leg_e:$90\text{ m}$ east], then turns and walks [leg_n:$80\text{ m}$ north], and finally walks [leg_w:$30\text{ m}$ west] to the library.

Find the total [dist:distance] walked and the student's [disp:displacement] (magnitude and direction).

sections.title: Break the walk into axes
sections.note: choose east as $+x$ and north as $+y$

rows.note: along $-x$: adds $+30\text{ m}$ to [dist:$d$], but $-30\text{ m}$ to [dx:$\Delta x$]
compare path length with straight-line vector

sections.title: Concept → Field
sections.concept: Every step increases [dist:distance], whereas opposite steps cancel along each axis before perpendicular axes combine by {pythagoras_disp|Pythagoras} into [disp:displacement].
sections.field: Kinematics (straight-line and 2D motion). Built on {dist_disp|distance and displacement} and {vectors|vectors and components}.

sections.title: Plan

routes.title: Route A
routes.path: sum lengths for [dist:$d$]; group [dx:$\Delta x$] and [dy:$\Delta y$] → {pythagoras_disp|Pythagoras} → [disp:$\Delta\vec{x}$]
routes.why: East and west lie on one line ($+x$/$-x$), and north is perpendicular ($+y$), so components simplify the geometry cleanly.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. This works for any multi-leg path.

routes.title: Route B
routes.path: add and subtract all three numbers directly: $90 + 80 - 30$
routes.why: West is opposite to east, so subtracting $30$ feels natural.
routes.whyNot: You cannot add north ($80\text{ m}$) directly to net east ($60\text{ m}$) as if they pointed the same way: $60 + 80 = 140\text{ m}$ is NOT the straight-line length.

sections.notUsed: Not used: time. Finding distance and displacement needs only positions and path lengths, not how fast the student walked.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: hover a step to highlight the parts it uses

steps.move: Add the length of every leg to find total [dist:distance].
steps.why: {dist_disp|Distance} is a non-negative scalar, so turning west still adds $30\text{ m}$ of walking.
steps.whyNot: Do not subtract $30\text{ m}$ here: walking west never erases the steps already taken.

steps.move: Combine the east and west legs along the $x$-axis to get [dx:$\Delta x$].
steps.why: East ($+x$) and west ($-x$) point in opposite directions along the same axis, so they partially cancel.
steps.whyNot: Do not ignore the sign of the westward leg: $90 + 30 = 120\text{ m}$ would put the library $60\text{ m}$ too far east.

steps.why: No leg goes south, so the net north–south shift is simply $+80\text{ m}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not mix [dy:$\Delta y$] with [dx:$\Delta x$] yet—perpendicular components stay separate until the right-triangle step.

steps.move: Combine [dx:$\Delta x$] and [dy:$\Delta y$] with {pythagoras_disp|Pythagoras} to find [disp:displacement].
steps.why: A $60\text{ m}$ east leg and $80\text{ m}$ north leg form a $3\text{–}4\text{–}5$ right triangle with hypotenuse $100\text{ m}$ and direction $\tan\theta = 80/60 = 4/3$, or $\theta \approx 53^\circ$ north of east.
steps.whyNot: Never stop at $100\text{ m}$ alone: {dist_disp|displacement} is a vector, so always state its direction ($53^\circ$ north of east).

sections.title: Explore 1D backtracking: when curves split
sections.note: walk east at $v_1$ until $t_1$, then turn west at $v_2$ until $10\text{ s}$

curves.expr: v1 * min(x, t1) + v2 * max(0, x - t1)
curves.label: [dist:distance $d(t)$] (always rises)

curves.expr: v1 * min(x, t1) - v2 * max(0, x - t1)
curves.label: [disp:displacement $\Delta x(t)$] (bends back)

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Inequality check**: $|\Delta\vec{x}| = 100\text{ m} \le 200\text{ m} = d$. If your displacement ever comes out larger than your distance, recheck your arithmetic.
**Straight one-way trip**: in the plot above, set $v_2 = 0$—the two curves overlap completely because $|\Delta x| = d$ when you never turn around.
**{round_trip|Round trip}**: set $v_1 = 10$, $v_2 = 10$, and $t_1 = 5\text{ s}$—distance is $100\text{ m}$, while displacement drops to **zero**.
**Direction matters**: displacement is never complete without a sign ($+$/$-$) in 1D or an angle/compass bearing in 2D.

questions.q: A runner completes one full lap around a $400\text{ m}$ oval track and stops at the starting line. What are the distance $d$ and displacement magnitude $|\Delta\vec{x}|$?
questions.why: The path covered is $400\text{ m}$, but start and finish are the same point, so {round_trip|displacement is zero}.

questions.q: A cyclist rides $30\text{ m}$ east and then $40\text{ m}$ north. What is the magnitude of the displacement?
questions.why: East and north are perpendicular, so by {pythagoras_disp|Pythagoras}, $|\Delta\vec{x}| = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = \sqrt{2500} = 50\text{ m}$ (while $70\text{ m}$ is the distance).

questions.q: When does the magnitude of displacement equal the distance traveled ($|\Delta\vec{x}| = d$)?
options: When the object moves in a straight line without reversing direction
Whenever the object moves at constant speed
Whenever the object ends where it started
questions.why: Any curve or reversal makes the path longer than the straight arrow. Constant speed around a circle still has $|\Delta\vec{x}| < d$.

questions.q: Along a straight road with east as positive, a student walks $50\text{ m}$ east and then $80\text{ m}$ west. What is the displacement?
questions.why: $\Delta x = (+50) + (-80) = -30\text{ m}$, meaning $30\text{ m}$ west of the starting point (while distance is $130\text{ m}$).
